title.en: Krisa Gautami Taught by a Courtesan

region.zh: 呾叉始羅妓館（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XI, Krisa Gautami (Kah-gyur xi. 122-130)

summary.en: Gautama's daughter Krisa, taught woman's work by a courtesan, three times declares herself done - and each time the teacher stages a trap: who would give herself a broken head for a stranger's child? who jumps into a well for a stranger's child? - and last, offering milk mixed secretly with oil and honey, then demanding the girl drink what she knows is loathsome. Driven out, Krisa learns that her schooling was in the arts of the courtesan's trade, not in any craft.
summary.zh: 吉祥生母（喬達彌）從妓學女子之藝，三度自稱學成，三度被師父設計拆穿——誰會為陌生孩子砸破自己的頭？誰會為陌生孩子跳井？最後以摻油蜜的酸乳相試，令其飲下「明知可憎之物」。逐出師門，方知學的原是妓家的手段。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur narrative literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: When the girl said she had acquired what was to be learnt and would go away, the woman took a paint-box and declared she would give herself a broken head if the girl was determined to go; then, when Krisa promised to remain, she said: you believed you had learnt everything, and yet did not know this - who would give herself a broken head for the sake of a stranger child? The same test was repeated with a well: no one jumps into a well for the sake of a strange child.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Krisa Gautami (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The woman brought milk and, in the girl's presence, mixed oil and honey with it, drank some, rendered it loathsome, and told her to drink. When Krisa refused, the woman cried before the neighbours - wherefore should I give her what is loathsome? - and the neighbours set seriously to work to make the girl drink; but when she was going to, the woman seized her hand and slapped her: if you had learnt all that was to be learnt, you would never have let that be given you which you knew was loathsome. Consequently you know nothing. Having thus spoken she drove the girl away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Krisa Gautami (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Raven's Beak and the Long Nose

region.en: River bank near Varanasi (Kah-gyur narrative India, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 波羅奈河畔（迦起律典敘事，象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XI, Krisa Gautami

summary.en: Stripped of his goods by the courtesan who posed as his bride, the ruined merchant watches a raven lengthen its beak by rubbing it on one wood and shorten it on another - and buys both kinds. Returning with five hundred Karshapanas he buys back the courtesan's friendship, rubs her nose long, lets all the doctors fail, and restores it only when she returns his property: soon come to an end the means of him who resides in two places.
summary.zh: 破產的商人目睹渡鴉以木擦喙——一木令喙變長，一木令喙復原——便買下兩種木。他攜五百金回到妓處「重修舊好」，把她的鼻子擦長；群醫束手，直到她歸還全部財物才替她復原：「寄居兩處者，資財速盡。」

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur narrative literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: At a river the merchant saw a corpse floating and a raven on the bank unable to reach it with its beak; it rubbed its beak on a piece of wood, and the beak lengthened, and it fed; on another piece of wood the beak returned to its former length. The merchant took pieces of the two woods home, bought the courtesan's friendship with five hundred Karshapanas, rubbed the wood on her nose - which became very long - and all the doctors could do nothing. Only when she promised to restore his property did he rub it with the second wood and make it as it had been.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Krisa Gautami (1882); not verbatim.

region.en: Flooded road to Varanasi and its cemeteries (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 通往波羅奈的水路與屍林（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XI, Krisa Gautami

summary.en: Traveling to her parents for her second confinement, Krisa's husband sleeps under a tree and is bitten by a snake; a thief takes the oxen; crossing the flooded river in two trips, she loses one son to a jackal while waving at it and the other to the steep bank as he springs to her call; a hurricane has meanwhile destroyed her parents' house. Remarried to a brutal weaver, she is forced by him to boil her newborn in oil and eat its flesh; she flees to a caravan, whose leader is killed by robbers, then to the robber-chief, killed by the king; taken into the zenana, she is buried alive in the king's tomb, escapes when grave-robbers' dust makes her sneeze, and wandering mad reaches Sravasti, where the Buddha gives her a robe, teaches her, and makes her chief of the Bhikshunis.
summary.zh: 吉祥生母攜子返娘家待產，丈夫樹下被蛇咬死；渡洪水分兩次抱子，一子被豺叼走，一子因撲向母親墜岸而亡；父母一家又遭颶風滅門。改嫁粗暴織工，被迫將新生兒投入沸油並食其肉；逃出後隨商隊，首領死於強盜，轉嫁盜首，盜首又死於王，入王后宮；王死後被活埋於王陵，因盜墓者揚塵使其打噴嚏而得脫。瘋癲流浪至舍衛城，佛陀賜衣、說法，立她為比丘尼之首。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur narrative literature; the infanticide and sati-like burial are elements of the traditional tale, reported factually and without endorsement.

passages.text: Her husband, asleep under a tree while she bore her child in the waggon, was bitten by a snake and died; a thief carried off the oxen. Crossing the flooded river in two journeys, she seated the elder boy on the bank and carried the younger over; while she stood in mid-stream waving at the jackal that seized the younger, the elder sprang into the water at her call, fell down the steep bank, and was killed. Bereft of husband and children, she learned that a hurricane had destroyed her parents with all their domestics.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Krisa Gautami (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Remarried to a rough, passionate weaver who beat her, she was driven on the night of her confinement to light a fire and boil oil, and to throw the new-born babe in; when it was cooked he ordered her to take it out and eat its flesh, and beat her until she did. When his rage was appeased and he slept, she took what food she could carry and went away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Krisa Gautami (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Her caravan-leader husband was killed fighting robbers, the robber-chief who took her was killed by the king, and she was transferred to the zenana; when the king died she was buried alive in his tomb with great honour. Grave-robbers from the north broke in, the dust made her sneeze, they fled thinking her a Vetala, and she escaped through their opening; out of her mind, covered with her underclothing, she wandered until she reached Sravasti, where at the sight of Bhagavant she recovered her intellect. He had Ananda give her an over-robe, taught her the doctrine, admitted her into the ecclesiastical body, and appointed her chief of the Bhikshunis.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Krisa Gautami (1882); not verbatim.

title.zh: 蘇殊羅尼與鳥王金翅鳥

region.en: Kaserudvipa, island of the bird-king (symbolic pin in the eastern ocean)
region.zh: 迦葉波洲鳥王之島（象徵定位於東海）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XII, Susroni (Kah-gyur xi. 93-99)

summary.en: Shipwrecked on a plank, a merchant's wife is carried to Kaserudvipa and wedded by the bird-king Suparna; she bears him a boy and a young bird. On her insistence the young bird-king seats his elder brother on the throne of Varanasi in place of the human king Brahmadatta, carried off and flung into the sea - with a warning to the ministers. The deposed king begs his bird-brother's help from time to time.
summary.zh: 商人之妻海難漂流至迦葉波洲，為鳥王金翅鳥所娶，生一子一雛。雛鳥繼位為鳥王後，應母親之請，抓走凡人國王梵授投入大海，改立兄長為波羅奈王，並警告群臣：誰敢作惡，下場如梵授。新王求助於鳥弟，時時往來。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur narrative literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: The wife escaped on a plank and was driven by the wind to Kaserudvipa, where dwelt the bird-king Suparna, who made her his wife; she bore him first a very beautiful boy and then a young bird Suparna, who after his father's death was installed king of the birds. His mother insisted on his installing his elder brother as king in Varanasi, so he carried off King Brahmadatta in his claws, flung him into the sea, set his own brother on the throne arrayed in all splendour, and warned the ministers that he would treat any one of them who did the least thing wrong exactly like Brahmadatta.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Susroni (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Truth-Asseveration and Susroni's Daily Flight
title.zh: 實語咒誓與蘇殊羅尼的每日飛行

region.en: Zenana of Varanasi and the sky to Kaserudvipa (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 波羅奈後宮與飛往迦葉波洲的天空（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XII, Susroni

summary.en: The king's elephant cannot bring forth; neither the royal wives' asseverations nor their presence help, but a mere herdswoman's oath - 'if it is true that one husband is sufficient for me and I have not two husbands, let the elephant be eased' - works on the spot. Judging all his wives of vicious habits, the king weds the herdswoman's daughter Susroni, and to keep her pure has Suparna carry her daily to Kaserudvipa and back by night; every day the bird brings him wreaths of the odorous Timira flower.
summary.zh: 王象難產，王妃們的咒誓無效，一名牧牛女只以一句「我若真只有一個丈夫」的實語，象即產下。王判定后妃皆有淫行，娶牧牛女之女蘇殊羅尼，又恐她近墨而黑，命金翅鳥每日載她往返迦葉波洲，夜歸王宮；金翅鳥每日獻上島上的提彌羅香花環。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur narrative literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: Although the elephant was introduced into the zenana and the wives pronounced their asseverations, the pains did not come to an end; a woman looking after oxen near the palace declared that by her asseveration the pains would cease, and said: if it is true that one husband is sufficient for me, and I have not two husbands, then as the result of this truth let the elephant be eased of its pains. Immediately after this utterance the elephant brought forth, and the king declared all his wives of vicious habits.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Susroni (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: He took the herdswoman's daughter Susroni as his wife, but fearing she would contract bad habits among the other women of the court, begged the bird-king Suparna to convey her every day to Kaserudvipa and bring her back every night; Suparna agreed, and sent him every day wreaths of the odorous Timira flower which grew at Kaserudvipa.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Susroni (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Asuga's Cave, His Lute, and the Doomed String
title.zh: 阿輸伽的石穴、琵琶與致命之弦

region.en: Kinnari's rocky grot in the forest (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 林中緊那羅的岩穴（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XII, Susroni

summary.en: A Kinnari hides a wood-gathering Brahman youth in a rocky grot, barring the entrance with a block he cannot move, and bears him a son, Asuga - Swiftfoot - who trains lifting ever-larger stones until he can shift the barrier. His mother's parting gift is a lute that sustains life - but its uppermost string must never be touched. At the Pandit's demand Asuga plays and touches it: the whole house skips with a crash, pots break, and he is turned out; later, playing on board a merchant ship, he touches it again at the merchants' request, and the ship bounds into the air and capsizes, drowning them all while Asuga is carried on a plank to Kaserudvipa.
summary.zh: 緊那羅將拾柴的婆羅門青年藏於岩穴，以巨石封門，生下疾足之子阿輸伽。少年日日舉石練力，終能移開封石，與父逃回波羅奈。母親贈琵琶為生——惟最上一弦不可觸。經師強令演奏，觸弦之際全屋跳動崩裂、器皿盡碎，他被逐出；後在商船上又應眾商之請觸弦，船騰空傾覆，眾商溺斃，阿輸伽抱板漂至迦葉波洲。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur narrative literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: Whenever the Brahman youth left the cave for flowers and fruits, the Kinnari closed the entrance with a great block of stone; the boy Asuga began to lift masses of stone, a larger one every day, until he could move the block, and spat out the fruits he was given so that his mother would range farther for better ones. He pushed the rock aside, and father and son reached Varanasi; the mother, finding the cave empty, resolved to give her son the means of prolonging his life.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Susroni (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Her friends gave him a lute by which he could support himself, but told him not to touch its uppermost string, for doing so would entail a great misfortune. At the instigation of the Pandit he touched it: the Brahman and his wife began to skip and dance, the whole house skipped with a crash, and all the pots and crockery were broken to pieces. On board a merchant ship, playing at the merchants' request, he touched the top string again; the ship began to bound in the air and capsized, and Asuga, getting hold of a plank, was driven by a storm to Kaserudvipa.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Susroni (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Susroni Exiled, and the Jackal Who Speaks with Kings
title.zh: 蘇殊羅尼被逐與通王語之豺

region.en: Royal park of Varanasi, hill town, river Karada (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 波羅奈王苑、山鎮與迦羅陀河（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XII, Susroni

summary.en: Dalliance by day with Asuga and by night with the king leaves Susroni exposed when Asuga, blind from opening his eyes on Suparna's back, sings of her dwelling and marks - the svastika on her thigh, her spiral breast. The king gives her to the blind man and exiles both on one ass; in a temple that night a robber chief throws Asuga from the wall to the townsmen, takes his things, and abandons her naked at the flooded Karada. Mocked by a jackal who has lost both fish and flesh, she is told her virtue will come when the Ganges flows upward - but the jackal then petitions the king (whose tongue can read jackal-speech) and restores her to favor for a daily piece of meat.
summary.zh: 蘇殊羅尼晝與阿輸伽私會、夜侍國王；開眼致盲的阿輸伽在苑中聞香而歌，唱出她大腿上的卍字與胸前的螺紋。王怒，把她賜給盲人並同驢逐出城。夜宿空廟，盜魁將阿輸伽拋下牆任鎮民處死，捨她於迦羅陀河邊。嘲弄她的老豺（曾同失魚與肉）道盡「恆河倒流方顯你貞潔」，隨後卻替她向能通獸語的國王求情，使她復位——只是每日須奉肉一塊，不敢稍怠。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur narrative literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: Asuga, blind from opening his eyes on Suparna's back, sang in the park: set in movement by the wind the odour of the Timira is perceptible - this is Kaserudvipa, where Susroni dwells. Asked by the king in slokas what marks her body bore, he answered: on her thigh is the svastika, her breast is spiral, over her spread wreaths of Timira blossoms. The king gave Susroni arrayed in all splendour to the blind man and ordered both driven out of the city riding upon the same ass.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Susroni (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: In an empty temple that night the robber chief, hiding from the townsmen who had beaten off his five hundred, flung the blind man from the wall to be killed, and at the flooded Karada made Susroni swim naked while he went off with her things. Crawling into the grass, she scoffed at an old jackal that had lost both the fish and its piece of flesh; the jackal retorted in slokas - thy husband hast thou killed, thy paramour has fled - that her virtue would come when the Ganges flowed upwards and the raven had the colour of curdled milk. Then it asked what reward she would give if it restored her to her position, and she promised a piece of meat every day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Susroni (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Immersed to her neck with her face to the east while the jackal petitioned the king - for King Brahmadatta understood the language of the jackal - she was fetched back with clothes and ornaments and restored to her former position. Every day she gave the jackal a piece of meat, until she gave up doing so; then the jackal came close to the royal palace and threatened that if she failed to bring the gift it would set her back in the place she occupied before, and she was alarmed and continued the tribute.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Susroni (1882); not verbatim.

region.en: Venuvana, Rajagriha, and the ocean road (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 王舍城竹園與通海之路（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XIII, The Over-reached Actor (Kah-gyur vii. 221-229)

summary.en: Two Nagarajas whose waters make Rajagriha's five hundred warm springs and crops prosper are converted by the Buddha and wish to move to the ocean; told to ask King Bimbisara, they appear by day as householders - and when the king, piqued that they do not rise for him, banishes the 'householders', they pour down a mighty jet of water and go by canal and river to the ocean. The springs dry and the crops perish; the Buddha recalls to the king that the banished men were the Nagarajas, teaches him the proper obeisance, and the king builds two temples and founds a six-monthly festival at which multitudes from the six great cities gather.
summary.zh: 王舍城五泉賴二龍王而豐饒。二龍皈依佛陀後欲遷居大海，佛令其請示頻毘娑羅王；二龍白天現身為居士，王怒其見己不起，將「二居士」逐出國境。二龍化大水柱，經渠入河出海，泉水枯竭、莊稼凋零。佛陀為王點破原委，教以合掌請罪之禮；王遂建二龍神廟、創半年一度大節，六大城民眾雲集。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur narrative literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: When the two Nagarajas perceived the king from afar they asked Bhagavant whether they should pay honour to the excellent law or to the king; he answered: pay honour to the excellent law. They omitted to rise in the king's presence, and the king waxed angry; on his orders his servants told the 'householders' not to remain in the country, whereupon they produced a mighty jet of water and betook themselves by small canals into great canals, from small rivers into great rivers, and into the ocean.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Over-reached Actor (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The five hundred warm springs, the rivers, lakes and pools began to dry up and the crops to perish; the Buddha informed the king that the banished householders were the two Nagarajas, and taught him the forgiveness-rite - stretch out your right hand and say, forgive me. Pardoned, the Nagarajas agreed to return only when the king had erected two temples, provided them with attendants, and founded a festival to be held every six months at which they would appear in person; he obeyed, and at the festival vast multitudes came together from the six great cities.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Over-reached Actor (1882); not verbatim.

region.zh: 王舍城節慶戲棚（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XIII, The Over-reached Actor (Kah-gyur vii. 221-229)

summary.en: At the Nagaraja festival an actor from the south, hoping to glorify the Buddha for profit, begs the Bhikshus' accounts of his life; the monks refuse, but the learned Bhikshuni Sthulananda recites the whole Abhinishkramana-Sutra for a fee - conception as a white elephant, the quaking earth, the dark worlds illumined, Mara overcome by the wheel of mildness. The actor stages the drama, then - to convert unbelievers - mimics two Bhikshus begging food, with a dish of ashes crowned by lumps of sugar dumped on the Chhanda-actor's head, and the crowd laughs the unbelievers into faith. But the mocked Six Bhikshus mount a rival booth with palace raiment; the astonished actor, thinking he watches gods and Nagas, follows them out and is forced to surrender his takings.
summary.zh: 南方伶人欲編佛陀生平安以牟利，諸比丘拒而不答，博學的比丘尼梭盧那陀收費後把《出家經》從白象入胎、大地震動、暗處光明，到以柔輪伏魔成道，一一道盡。伶人據此演劇，又添「乞食」一幕——以灰碗上放糖塊，倒於扮闡陀者頭上——連不信者也笑而至信。但被醜化的六群比丘借來宮中服飾，在鄰棚演出；伶人以為目睹天龍夜叉之神戲，驚駭追出，被迫獻出全部所得。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur narrative literature; a rare early testimony to Buddhist sacred drama; living tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: Sthulananda, very learned and knowing the Tripitaka thoroughly, related everything in full out of the Abhinishkramana-Sutra: dwelling in the Tushita region the Bodhisat appointed the five meditations, and having allowed the six Kamavachara gods to receive purification three times, he consciously entered the mother's womb transformed into the shape of an elephant, whereupon the great earth quaked and the darkness of the world-intervals was profusely illumined anew.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Over-reached Actor (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The actor pitched a booth in Rajagriha on the day of the Nagaraja festival and exhibited the events of the Buddha's life; then, to create faith among unbelievers, he introduced one actor as Udayin and another as Chhanda with a dish of ashes topped by two or three lumps of sugar - the Udayin-actor ate the sugar and upset the ashes over the other's head, saying, take and go. The crowd burst out laughing loudly, and even the unbelieving became believing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Over-reached Actor (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Six Bhikshus, mocked in his play, took ornaments and raiment from the palace, set up a booth close to his, and performed; the actor thought he was witnessing a divine drama, performed by Gods, Nagas, Yakshas, Gandharvas, Kinnaras or Mahoragas. Followed out and caught, Udayin told him plainly: as you have brought us on to the stage, we will go to every place where you perform and annoy you - and the actor, begging pardon, had to give up the whole of his receipts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Over-reached Actor (1882); not verbatim.

region.en: Brahmavati lake and the forest grave-pit, Varanasi (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 波羅奈梵摩提湖與林中墓坑（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XIV, The Dumb Cripple (Kah-gyur vi. 89-99)

summary.en: A being of firm resolve comes out of hell into the childless King Brahmadatta's queen and is born on the water of the Brahmavati lake - Abja, water-born - remembering a former sixty-year reign that cost sixty thousand years in hell. To escape the throne he feigns first lameness, then dumbness; three times handed to the executioners he asks only riddling questions - is Varanasi inhabited? is this corpse of a living man or a dead man? would this grain-heap not wax great but for being devoured at its base? - and each time returns speechless, until the digging of the forest grave-hole draws from him a verse, a bargain, and finally speech: a plain account of the hell he fled, and three parables on the death he fears.
summary.zh: 一個從地獄脫出、誓願堅固的眾生投生於無子之王后胎中，因生於梵摩提湖上而名「水生」阿波闍——他猶記前生六十年為王、隨後在地獄受刑六萬年。為逃王位先裝跛後裝啞；三度交與劊子手，只問謎語——王城有人居否？此屍屬死人還是活人？穀堆若不從底部被吃能長多大？——三次無言而歸，直到林中掘墓方出偈求免，最後開口自陳地獄之痛，並以三喻答王。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur narrative literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: As he rapidly grew up he reflected that if he were invested with sovereign power, this would not be a good thing, seeing that for a sixty years reign in a previous state of existence he had been born again in hell, and that he now ran the risk of going to hell a second time; he pretended to be a cripple, and when his father persisted, pretended to be dumb, and was commonly called the Dumb Cripple.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Dumb Cripple (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Handed to the executioners, he asked only whether the great city was deserted or inhabited, whether a carried corpse was the body of a living man or a dead man, and whether a grain-heap continually devoured at its base would not wax great; each time he was brought back speechless, and the king finally ordered him buried in a hole in the forest. At the digging he spoke his sloka, bargained for one wish - and entered the city on foot declaring, I am neither dumb nor crippled; sound and clear and bright is my mind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Dumb Cripple (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: He explained the three sayings: no one ventured to ask why the king condemned his own son to death without cause; the corpse of a criminal is the corpse of one dead, but of him who has done good it is the corpse of one alive; and as tillers who stop on the path of virtue have the roots of their earlier virtue severed and pass from the path of bliss into perdition, so the grain-heap devoured at its base can never wax great. The king embraced him with tearful eyes, allowed him to renounce the world with all his young companions, and he became known as the Dumb Teacher, teaching his disciples contentment with only what is most necessary.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Dumb Cripple (1882); not verbatim.

region.en: Hermitage in a villageless forest; ferry-boat pleasure-ground (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 無村野林之淨修林與渡船行宮（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XV, Rshyasringa (Kah-gyur iv. 136-137)

summary.en: A penance-performing Rishi is made father by a gazelle doe that comes to his late dwelling-place; her terrified doe deserts the horned boy, whom the Rishi rears as Rshyasringa, Gazelle-horn. The boy inherits the five insights, and his curse on the rain-deity - for breaking his water-pitcher - shuts off the rain for twelve years and empties Varanasi. The king's daughter Santa leads a fleet of bark-dressed women aboard a ferry-boat hermitage, lures the forest youth aboard with wine-filled fruits, and unfettered rain follows his captivation - until the Rishi, beaten by Santa's shoe in a jealousy quarrel, reclaims his five insights by renewed austerities.
summary.zh: 苦行仙人使前來其舊居的母鹿懷孕；母鹿驚懼棄子，仙人收養頭生鹿角之兒，名鹿角仙人。少年得五神通，因雨神打破他的水罐而詛咒十二年不雨，波羅奈大饑，百姓四散。王女商陀率一船披樹皮的女人設行宮為餌，以釀酒之果誘其登船；仙人墮愛而法力盡失，天即降雨。後因妒忌爭吵被商陀以鞋擊頭，仙人再度苦行，重獲五通。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur narrative literature; a Buddhist version of the Rishyasringa story known from the Mahabharata and Ramayana, noted by Schiefner.

passages.text: A gazelle doe came to a spot where the Rishi had lately been and became pregnant; at the birth she smelt the child, perceived it did not resemble herself, and deserted it. The Rishi perceived it was his own child, took it into his hermitage, and named it Rshyasringa, Gazelle-horn, when gazelle horns appeared on the boy's head.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Rshyasringa (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Fetching water in a full pitcher, the youth let it fall in the rain; Rishis are very quickly moved to wrath, and he reproached the deity: as my full water pitcher has been broken in consequence of your bad behaviour, you shall not let rain fall for twelve years from this day. A great famine arose in Varanasi, and its inhabitants emigrated; the diviners declared that if the Rishi could be disturbed in his penances the deity would again send rain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Rshyasringa (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The king's daughter Santa had herself and other women taught mystic lore by the Brahmans, had a hermitage prepared on a ferry-boat, and, dressed in bark and grass like a Rishi, went to the boy's hermitage - where he noticed at once that a loosely flowing step, a face free from beard and a rising and falling breast were no Rishi's appearance. On the boat they spread stupefying substances and cocoa-nuts filled with wine; intoxicated and seduced, he gave himself up to pleasure with the women, and his magic power vanished as the deity rejoicing in rain called the clouds together. Given Santa as wife, he wandered from her to other women until, struck on the head with a shoe in a wrangle, he recalled that he who once overbore the thunder of the clouds was now set at nought by a woman - and again devoted himself to ascetic exertion, becoming once more possessed of the five kinds of insight.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Rshyasringa (1882); not verbatim.

region.en: Visvanagara city and the road to the penance-forest (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 須大拏城與通往苦行林之路（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XVI, Visvantara (Kah-gyur iv. 192-200)

summary.en: The Bodhisattva prince Visvantara gives away his jewelled chariot to Veda-Brahmans and then the rain-making white elephant Rajyavardhana; his furious father exiles him. Madri, who cannot live a single instant parted from him, goes with him into the penance-forest with their two children, refusing his warning about roots and thorns; at three hundred yojanas another Brahman claims the chariot as recompense for his fatigue, and Visvantara, teaching his angry wife that without covetous men there would be no giving, bestows it a second time.
summary.zh: 菩薩太子須大拏先施寶車，再施能致雨的白象軍持；父王一怒將其逐出。王妃摩坻自言離他一刻也活不成，攜二子同往苦行林。行至三百由旬，又一婆羅門討車，摩坻怒斥其無憐憫，太子卻教誨她「無貪婪者便無布施」，再度施車。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur narrative literature; the Wessantara Jataka, central to Himalayan and Southeast Asian Buddhist devotion; living tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: Riding out in a chariot gleaming with jewels, gold, silver, coral, lapis-lazuli, turquoises, rubies and sapphires, Visvantara alighted swiftly and gave it to the Veda-Brahmans who asked it, saying, as I have given away the chariot with the greatest pleasure, so may I, giving away the three worlds, become possessed of the greatest insight. Later he gave the white elephant Rajyavardhana, in whiteness equalled only by jasmine, snow and silver, to discussing Brahmans - and his father, angry at the news, sent for him and ordered him to quit the country.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Visvantara (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Madri joined her palms and said she was not capable of living a single instant parted from him, as the sky deprived of the moon, as the earth deprived of water, so is the wife deprived of her husband; refusing his warning of grass-beds and thorns, she followed him, and hundreds of thousands of townsfolk attended their lamenting departure. At three hundred yojanas a Brahman claimed the chariot as recompense for his fatigue; Madri railed at him, but Visvantara said, find no fault - if there were no people who long after riches, there would be no giving - and bestowed the chariot with exceeding great joy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Visvantara (1882); not verbatim.

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XVI, Visvantara

summary.en: While Madri gathers roots, a Brahman claims the two children as slaves; Visvantara reasons that if he would give his own life he cannot hesitate over his children, and though the earth quakes sixfold at the surrender he gives them, with tears, for the redemption of the world. The children beg to see their mother first, ask his forgiveness as for children's faults, and circle him three times, looking back tearfully - while gods shout in the air that he is worthy of wonder whose mind stays constant even after the surrender of both his children.
summary.zh: 摩坻采果期間，一婆羅門索要兩個孩子為奴。須大拏自忖：若連自身性命都肯施，豈能猶豫於子女？雖大地六次震動，他仍含淚交出，以救度世間。孩子求見母親一面，認錯告饒，繞父三匝，一步三回頭——空中諸神齊聲讚嘆：子女盡施而其心不動，誠可驚嘆。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur narrative literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: The Brahman who wandered alone with his staff claimed the two children as slaves, and pressed the hesitating prince: you are renowned all over the earth as the possessor of a compassion which gives away all things. Visvantara answered that if he had to give away his own life he would not hesitate for a single moment, and gave the children - whereupon the earth quaked in a sixfold manner, and an old ascetic read the omen: the earth has been set in movement because Visvantara has given up his two beloved children that he may redeem men reduced to despair.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Visvantara (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The children touched his feet, begging to be given up only after they had seen their mother, then asked forgiveness for their faults as children and, having paid reverence and three times encompassed him, went forth ever looking back with tearful eyes. Scarcely had they gone when the system of the three thousand worlds quaked six times, and thousands of gods filled the air with shouting: oh the great deed of surrender! truly is he worthy of being wondered at, whose mind remains constant even after the surrender of both his children.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Visvantara (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Madri Given and Restored: Sakra's Test
title.zh: 摩坻被施與歸還：帝釋之試

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XVI, Visvantara

summary.en: Returning with roots, Madri reads the omens - twitching eye, wailing birds, quaking earth - and knows her children are given away; she searches the children's planted trees and young gazelle playfellows, then collapses like a gazelle pierced by a poisoned arrow. Sakra, admiring both husband and wife, comes as a Brahman and asks for Madri herself; Visvantara gives her with a contented mind, and the earth quakes again - until Sakra lays aside his disguise, grants Madri her wish for her children's freedom, and returns her to her husband with the charge: what is entrusted must not be given away.
summary.zh: 摩坻歸來，見眼跳、聞鳥哀、覺地震，已知兒女被施；她撫孩子種的樹、尋伴孩子玩耍的小羚羊，終如中箭之鹿倒地。帝釋感其夫婦之德，化身婆羅門索討摩坻；須大拏欣喜施之，大地再震——帝釋現出真身，滿摩坻「釋放子女使其歸祖父」之願，把妻子交還丈夫，並囑咐：受託之物不可再施。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur narrative literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: A deity who perceived she might hinder the surrender assumed the form of a lioness and barred her way, turning aside only at her words about similar rank; then, reading her twitching eye, the wailing notes and the quaking earth, Madri knew both her children had been given away, embraced the trees the children had planted and tended, and found their interrupted footprints leading in all directions like dragging.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Visvantara (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The king of the gods, Sakra, resolved to ask for Madri, and took the form of a Brahman; Madri raged at the shameless suitor, but Visvantara gave her without hesitation, and when in order to attain supreme insight he had given away his beautiful wife the earth quaked six times to its extremities like a boat on the water. Then Sakra laid aside his Brahman's form and asked Madri what she desired: that he would set her children free from thraldom and let them find their way to their grandfather. Taking Madri by the left hand he gave her back: you must not give her to any one - if you give away what has been entrusted to you, fault will be found with you.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Visvantara (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Children Sold to Their Grandfather

region.en: Main street and palace of Visvanagara (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 須大拏城大街與王宮（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XVI, Visvantara

summary.en: Sakra deludes the Brahman into selling the children in the very city they left; the ministers recognize the royal grandchildren, destitute of clothing and foul of body, and the king falls from his throne to the ground. Summoning Visvantara and Madri, he installs the Bodhisattva as king after Visvamitra's death, and the All-giver Visvantyaga endows Sramanas, Brahmans, the poor and needy of every caste, proclaiming in slokas that giving is the most excellent of virtues. The enriched Brahman Jujuka, asked to honor his benefactor, answers that he owes his wealth to his own first-caste birth.
summary.zh: 帝釋迷惑婆羅門，使其將孩子賣回原來的城市；群臣認出衣不蔽體的龍孫，老王自寶座跌落。須大拏夫婦被迎回；父王死後，菩薩被立為王，號「一切施」。他普施四姓、施及貧苦，誦偈宣揚布施為最勝之德。而因他而暴富的婆羅門朱閻伽卻說：我的財富全憑我第一種姓的福報，與太子何干。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur narrative literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: The king of the gods deluded the Brahman so that, under the impression it was another city, he entered the selfsame city and set to work to sell the children; the ministers recognized the royal grandchildren Krishna and Jalini, destitute of clothing and with foul bodies, and the king fell from his throne to the ground while all present wept. He ordered the bright-eyed giver summoned with his wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Visvantara (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: When King Visvamitra died the Brahmans, ministers, townspeople and country people went to the hermitage and invited the Bodhisat to the city, installing him as king under the name of Visvantyaga, the All-giver; after endowing Sramanas, Brahmans, the poor and needy of all castes with gold, silver, oxen, horses, jewelled earrings and slaves, he uttered his slokas: for giving is the most excellent of virtues - with a heart free from passion have I given away my wife and children, and obtained power over men in this and the other world. And the Brahman Jujaka, grown wealthy by the king's treasures, told his relations that what had he to do with Visvantara - he owed his wealth to his own birth in the first caste.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, Visvantara (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Fulfilled Prophecy of the Fisher-Lad Poet

region.zh: 波羅奈及其荒野（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XVII, The Fulfilled Prophecy (Kah-gyur iv. 233-236)

summary.en: Diviners doom Dharmika's unborn son to kill the king; Queen Suryanemi spares the mother until the birth, then has the boy swapped for a fisherman's daughter and raised as the verse-writing fisher-lad. Discovered, he escapes a mustard-oil bier, escapes pursuit by wearing shoes with the toes and heels reversed, is conveyed by the Nagas, defeats the flesh-eating Yaksha Pingala by throwing his garment down for the dogs to devour their master instead, loses his head-dress down a precipice, and finally - armed with his uncle's spell for changing sex - enters Varanasi as an incomparably beautiful woman, kills the king, reverses the spell, and takes the crown.
summary.zh: 相者預言王妃所懷之子將弒君奪位。王延至分娩，把男嬰與漁家女調換，孩子以「會作詩的漁童」之名長大。事發後他先是躺著芥子芝麻油塗身、被當屍體抬出；再訂做腳尖腳跟顛倒之鞋穿出城，追蹤者循「倒行」足跡返回村中；投水為龍王所救；在辟伽羅荒野以衣服拋下餵犬，令群犬反噬食肉羅剎；跳崖時被揪落頭巾，追者誤為已死。最後憑叔父傳授的變性咒化作絕色女子入城，伺機弒王，反咒復形，戴上王冠。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur narrative literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: Goshthila, charged with Dharmika's safety, exchanged her newborn son for a fisherman's daughter the same day, and the boy was brought up by the fisherwoman as the verse-writing fisher-lad. When the longing queen had him sent to her with a fish, the king recognized the doomed child and ordered him seized; hidden by an old woman, he was carried out anointed with oil of mustard and sesame upon a bier as if a corpse, and deposited in the cemetery.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Fulfilled Prophecy (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: He escaped pursuers in a clothes-chest on an ass, then ordered shoes with the toes where the heels generally are - manifold is the mind, numerous are gifts, they cannot be weighed in the same scale - and crept out through a cistern, so that the traces left by his shoes led his followers back to the village. Conveyed by the Nagas, he fled the snake-charmers' spells into the Pingala wilderness, where he escaped the flesh-eating Yaksha by throwing down part of his clothes from the tree; the dogs, taking them for the youth, ate up the Yaksha himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Fulfilled Prophecy (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Leaping down a precipice as the king's men closed in, he left his head-dress in a seizing hand, and the pursuers reported the fisher-lad poet dead. His uncle, the retired Rishi, taught him the spell by which a man might be turned into a woman and back; the youth assumed the form of an incomparably beautiful woman, was seen in the king's park, brought to the palace, and violently enamoured the king - then, at an opportunity, put Suryanemi to death in a solitary spot, reversed the spell, and assumed the regal power. A deity sang: he whose head has not been cut off is not dead - he gets up again and completes his work.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Fulfilled Prophecy (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Two Brothers: Kshemankara and Papankara
title.zh: 兄弟二人：吉祥莊嚴與罪業莊嚴

region.en: Island of Jewels and the ocean road (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 寶洲與航海之路（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XVIII, The Two Brothers (Kah-gyur iv. 186-189)

summary.en: Born amid thousands of happy events, Kshemankara the generous goes to sea; Papankara, born amid misfortunes and jealous of his brother's love, follows to murder him. When a sea-monster wrecks the ship, the good brother carries the bad ashore and sleeps exhausted - and Papankara steals his girdle-jewels and puts out both his eyes with a thorn. Blind, saved by herdsmen, refusing the herdsman's wife's advances, Kshemankara plays the lute through the markets; the princess who was to have been his long ago chooses him by the lute's sound before all the princes, and restores one eye by the truth of her love and the other by his truth that he bears no malice. The neighboring king marches, drives out Papankara, and sets Kshemankara on his father's throne.
summary.zh: 吉祥莊嚴生時千祥雲集，慷慨樂施，泛海經商；罪業莊嚴生時災異頻仍，妒忌兄長得人心，隨行謀害。海怪毀船，善兄背惡弟上岸，力竭而眠——惡弟竊其腰間寶石，以刺刺瞎其雙目。失明的兄長被牧人救起，拒牧人之妻引誘，以琴聲行乞於市。昔日許婚的公主在擇婿大會上聞琴擲冠，先以實語咒誓復其一眼，又因其「不懷怨恨」的實語復其二目。鄰國起兵逐弟，立兄於父位。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur narrative literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: On the Island of Jewels the steersman let the merchants fill the ship with precious stones, and the wise Kshemankara fastened large jewels to his girdle; on the way home a sea-monster rendered the ship useless, and Papankara, throwing his arms round his brother's neck, was carried ashore by his exertions. While Kshemankara lay sleeping, exhausted by the burden, Papankara took away the jewels from his girdle, put both his eyes out with a thorn, and left him sightless on the ocean shore.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Two Brothers (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Oxherds led the blinded prince to the chief herdsman's house, where he took to playing on the lute; the chief's wife, charmed by his youth and beauty, tried to allure him, and he closed his ears - whereupon she told her husband the blind man was trying to tempt her, and he went away, gaining a living by his music through the streets and market places.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Two Brothers (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The princess, told that the prince intended for her had died at sea, asked to choose a husband herself; moved by the sound of the lute, she threw the crown of flowers on the blind player crying, this man is my husband. To silence the court's scorn he asseverated with her: if my love has been only for her, may one of my eyes become sound - and one eye came again as before. Then she proved her constancy, and he asseverated that although Papankara put out his eyes he bore him no malice - and the other eye became sound. With a great army the princess's father drove out Papankara and set Kshemankara upon his father's throne.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Two Brothers (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Poisoned Banquet of the Five Hundred Robbers

region.en: Elephant carcass by the forest road (Kah-gyur narrative India, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 林道旁的死象（迦起律典敘事，象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XIX, The Punishment of Avarice (Kah-gyur iii. 103)

summary.en: Five hundred robbers find a hunter's poisoned-arrow elephant and divide the work; but each half covets the whole - the cooks poison the leftover meat, the water-fetchers poison the leftover water - and all die. A jackal, fettered by the ties of time, sees the feast and, seizing a bow in its jaws to gnaw the bowstring knots, is killed when the string snaps against the roof of its mouth: it is good to accumulate, but not to accumulate immoderately.
summary.zh: 五百盜賊獲得獵人毒箭所斃的大象，分兩班燒肉取水；兩班各自毒殺對方——剩肉下毒、剩水下毒——全數斃命。一隻受時運縛束的豺見屍橫遍地，狂喜之下銜弓啃弦，弓弦崩斷擊中上顎而死：「積聚可也，過度不可。」

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur fable literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: The flesh-cooks resolved not to share with the others: let us eat as much of the meat as we please and poison the rest, and when they had eaten their fill they poisoned what remained; those who had fetched water likewise poisoned what was left. So when they came back, and those who had eaten the flesh drank the water and those who had drunk the water ate the flesh, they all died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Punishment of Avarice (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: A jackal, fettered by the ties of time, saw the dead bodies and thought that an extremely large amount of booty had accrued to it; seizing the bow with its jaws it began to gnaw at the knots of the bowstring, the string snapped, and the end of the bow struck the roof of its mouth so hard that it died. Its sloka: it is good to accumulate, but not to accumulate immoderately - see how the jackal, infatuated by greed after the accumulated, was killed by the bow.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, The Punishment of Avarice (1882); not verbatim.

region.en: Mountain, ravine and royal city (Kah-gyur narrative India, symbolic pin)
region.zh: 山地、澗谷與王城（迦起律典敘事，象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan Kah-gyur (translated c. 9th century), from Indian sources; Schiefner/Ralston translation 1882

source.work: Tibetan Tales Derived from Indian Sources, trans. Schiefner/Ralston (1882), ch. XXI, How a Woman Requites Love (Kah-gyur iv. 183-191)

summary.en: Four banished princes agree to kill their wives for food; Visakha, refusing to take another's life, flees with his own, slicing flesh from his hams and opening his veins to feed her. Rescuing a handless, footless man from the river, he lodges him with his wife - who seduces the cripple, then drops her husband down the wolf's-milk ravine by a feigned headache. Bodisat destiny makes him king of the city his stream carries him to, where he refuses all brides and reviles women; the barren mountain has driven his wife to beg with the cripple on her back, boasting 'my husband has never found fault with me' - until the king meets her with his own verse, and the ministers drive her out with contumely.
summary.zh: 四位被逐王子相約殺妻為食；毘捨怯寧捨己命不肯害人，攜妻而逃，割股肉、放臂血以餵之。他救起落水的斷手斷腳之人，交妻子照顧——妻子竟誘拐此人，又假稱頭痛，把取「狼乳」的丈夫用繩放下深澗，鬆手任其墜河。菩薩福報使順流而下的他被占卜者選為新王，登基後拒納后妃、痛斥婦人。那座山因他離開而百果枯萎，妻子背著殘廢者沿街乞討，自誇「丈夫從未責備過我」——直到國王以偈點破，群臣將她轟出城去。

sensitivity.note: Kah-gyur narrative literature; living Buddhist tradition treated respectfully.

passages.text: The four brothers made an agreement to put their wives to death one after another and feed on their flesh to make their way through the desert; Visakha thought it better to sacrifice his own life than to take away another's, and fled with his wife. Exhausted, she said she was dying, and he sliced flesh off his hams and gave it her to eat, opened the veins of both his arms and gave her the blood to drink.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, How a Woman Requites Love (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: He rescued from the river a man whose hands and feet had been cut off, satisfied his hunger, and handed him to his wife's care; living on the Bodisat-charged roots and berries, she allured the cripple, and in fear of discovery contrived the headache: as wolf's-milk grows in this ravine, I will let you down with a rope and you shall fetch it up. August beings are simple and upright; he suspected no guile, and she let go of the rope.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, How a Woman Requites Love (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Carried by the stream to a kingless city, he was found by the diviners sitting on a spot decked with ornaments, and was installed as king; but he refused all the brides brought to him and reviled women without ceasing. The mountain's roots and berries having shrivelled after his fall, his wife took the cripple on her back and begged alms boasting that her husband had never found fault with her - until the king met her and laughed out his verse: thou who hast eaten the flesh of my loins, who hast drunk my blood, who hast for the sake of wolf's-milk flung me down the precipice - wilt thou not now be blamed by thy husband? The ministers drove her out of the city with contumely.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schiefner/Ralston, How a Woman Requites Love (1882); not verbatim.
